In terms of knowledge, after completing this course students are able to:

1. Identify and explain the following topics:
  • three research paradigms: the positivist, interpretive and critical paradigms
  • three research methods: surveys, interviews and narrative analysis
  • empirical cycle
  • responsible research (e.g. ethical research, AI technologies for research purposes)
In terms of skills, after completing this course students are able to:
  1. Collaboratively perform and report specific steps of the empirical cycle, for one or more methods  (e.g., the literature search, formulating a research              question/hypothesis, data collection)  in small groups.
  2. Engage in and integrate open-minded and reflective dialogues regarding research methods grounded in diverse paradigmatic perspectives.
In terms of character, after completing this course students are able to:
  1. Acknowledge one’s own intuitions and prejudices when choosing and applying research methods  (critical mindset)
  2. Take a critical stance towards the normative aspects of research methods and research paradigms (intellectual independence)

What kind of knowledge do Culture Studies scholars produce? How does research in humanities and new media studies differ from other disciplines? What is methodology and how does it guide research? How are digital technologies employed responsibly in research design? How are interviews, surveys and narrative analysis employed in research in Culture Studies?

This course provides an introductory overview of methodology, major research paradigms and methods in the broader field of humanities and new media studies. Students will become familiar with three core research paradigms (positivist, interpretive, and critical paradigm) that can be identified in humanities and new media studies research. Students will be introduced to responsible research, including how to conduct research in an ethical way and how to use digital technologies in a responsible way. Students will gain insight into three main research methods (interview, survey and narrative analysis) that can be used to answer a variety of research questions. Students will be introduced into some of the skills needed to carry out research, and will apply their knowledge and skills by conducting their own research.

The course will start with a series of lectures about how methods relate to different research paradigms. We discuss the core building blocks of three major research paradigms, the positivist, interpretive and critical paradigm by focusing on their ontological, epistemological, and axiological foundations, and examine how these foundations bring forth certain methodologies of inquiry. Then we explore what responsible research is, how we design and conduct research in a transparent and ethical way and how we make use of digital technologies in research design in a responsible way. In the next part of the course, we take a closer look into different types of research (research methods). By employing the empirical cycle in collaborative group work, we discuss and implement how surveys, interviews and narrative analysis are conducted in culture studies. In this part, students work in collaborative groups to practice these methods by designing,  executing and reflecting on their own research ideas.
Cheek, J., & Øby, E. (2023). Research Design: Why Thinking about Design Matters. SAGE Publications.
